🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟭 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝘆 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮

Today, I focused on how real test environments work. Creating a table feels simple until you run the same script twice. On my second run in the sandbox, my screen threw a classic blocker: "table COUNTRY already exists."

That single error connected all three core concepts from my daily learning.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗖𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗧𝗘 𝗧𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘: Building the structure with exact column names and data types:
  CREATE TABLE COUNTRY (ID int, CCODE char(2), Name varchar(60));
🔹 𝗣𝗥𝗜𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗞𝗘𝗬 & 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗡𝗨𝗟𝗟: Locking IDs to stop duplicate rows. A database never allows empty values inside a Primary Key constraint:
  CREATE TABLE COUNTRY (ID int NOT NULL, CCODE char(2), Name varchar(60), PRIMARY KEY (ID));
🔹 𝗗𝗥𝗢𝗣 𝗧𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘: The standard practice of cleaning up old test tables right before creating fresh ones to avoid duplicate errors:
  DROP TABLE COUNTRY;

🚀 Day 2 of My Database Journey: Relational Model Constraints & Data Integrity

While studying database design today, I realized that creating a table is only half the job. Without strict rules on what data is allowed inside, a clean schema turns into a messy spreadsheet within weeks.

Using a 2-table BookShop schema, I practiced the 3 pillars of Data Integrity that protect databases from corrupted records and broken links.

💡 Core Concepts Learned Today:
🔹 Entity Integrity (Primary Key Rule): Ensures every table has a Primary Key so each row is distinct, unique, and never NULL:
  CREATE TABLE BookShop (BOOK_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, TITLE VARCHAR(100), AUTHOR_ID INT);
🔹 Referential Integrity (Foreign Key Rule): Ensures a Foreign Key in a child table always points to a valid Primary Key in a parent table, preventing orphaned records.
🔹 Domain Integrity (Data Validation Rules): Enforces rules on data types, mandatory fields (NOT NULL), and value ranges (CHECK constraint for valid limits).

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟯 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗔𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 (𝗟𝗜𝗞𝗘, 𝗕𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗘𝗘𝗡, 𝗜𝗡)

When you do not know the exact string stored in a table, or when you need to filter across 5 different countries, chaining endless '=' and 'OR' conditions makes a query hard to read and easy to break.

Today, I replaced long, messy filter chains with three clean SQL operators.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗟𝗜𝗞𝗘 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 (𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝘀): Uses the '%' wildcard to search for partial text patterns when you only know part of a value:
  SELECT firstname FROM author WHERE firstname LIKE 'R%';
🔹 𝗕𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗘𝗘𝗡 ... 𝗔𝗡𝗗 (𝗜𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗥𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀): Replaces long >= and <= conditions by filtering numbers or dates inclusively:
  SELECT * FROM Book WHERE pages BETWEEN 290 AND 300;
🔹 𝗜𝗡 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 (𝗦𝗲𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲𝘀): Filters multiple exact values in a single list instead of writing repetitive OR statements:
  SELECT * FROM author WHERE country IN ('Australia', 'Brazil');

📂 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆:

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟰 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗦𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗕𝗬

A basic SELECT query returns rows in whatever order the database engine reads them. Today, I focused on turning unsorted database rows into clean, ranked output using the ORDER BY clause.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗔𝘀𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿): By default, ORDER BY arranges text alphabetically (A to Z) and numbers from lowest to highest:
  SELECT title FROM book ORDER BY title;
🔹 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗖 𝗞𝗲𝘆𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱): Adding DESC at the end sorts results in reverse order (Z to A, or highest to lowest value):
  SELECT title FROM book ORDER BY title DESC;
🔹 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝘂𝗺𝗻 𝗦𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗡𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿: Instead of typing the full column name again, you can pass its position number from the SELECT list for faster ad-hoc querying:
  SELECT title, pages FROM book ORDER BY 2;

📂 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆:

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟱 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 & 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 (𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗖𝗧, 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗣 𝗕𝗬, 𝗛𝗔𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚)

Raw table dumps rarely answer business questions directly. Usually, we need unique lists, category counts, or filtered summaries. Today, I practiced summarizing 20 author rows across 6 countries and tackled the classic SQL question: WHERE vs. HAVING.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗗𝗜𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗖𝗧 (𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗗𝘂𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀): Collapses repeated column values into a clean list of unique entries:
  SELECT DISTINCT country FROM author ORDER BY 1;
🔹 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗣 𝗕𝗬 & 𝗔𝗦 (𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗹𝗶𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀): Buckets identical values together so aggregate functions like COUNT() can summarize each group with a clean column name:
  SELECT country, COUNT(country) AS Count FROM author GROUP BY country;
🔹 𝗛𝗔𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝘃𝘀. 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘: WHERE filters individual raw rows before grouping, while HAVING filters aggregated buckets after GROUP BY:
  SELECT country, COUNT(country) AS Count FROM author GROUP BY country HAVING COUNT(country) > 4;

📂 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆:

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟲 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁-𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (𝗔𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘃𝘀. 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿)

A single dirty text column with 'Cat', 'CAT', and 'cat' showed me why built-in SQL functions matter so much for real-world data cleaning.

Today, I worked with the PETRESCUE dataset to practice two core families of SQL functions: Aggregate functions and Scalar functions.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗔𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (𝗦𝗨𝗠, 𝗔𝗩𝗚, 𝗠𝗔𝗫, 𝗠𝗜𝗡): Take an entire column of values and return a single summary metric, even allowing math inside parentheses:
  SELECT AVG(COST / QUANTITY) FROM PETRESCUE WHERE ANIMAL = 'Dog';
🔹 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿 & 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗗, 𝗟𝗘𝗡𝗚𝗧𝗛, 𝗨𝗖𝗔𝗦𝗘, 𝗟𝗖𝗔𝗦𝗘): Operate on every individual value row-by-row:
  SELECT ROUND(COST), LENGTH(ANIMAL), UCASE(ANIMAL) FROM PETRESCUE;
🔹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲-𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 & 𝗡𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴: Converting messy text to lowercase inside WHERE ensures you never miss a row due to inconsistent capitalization:
  SELECT * FROM PETRESCUE WHERE LCASE(ANIMAL) = 'cat';

📂 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆:

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟳 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝗤𝗟

Every real analytics project eventually asks a time question: "How many rescues happened in May?" or "Which orders are more than 3 days overdue?" Today, I explored how relational databases store, slice, and calculate dates across DATE (YYYYMMDD), TIME (HHMMSS), and 20-digit TIMESTAMP formats.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀 (𝗗𝗔𝗬, 𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗛, 𝗬𝗘𝗔𝗥): Pulls out specific slices of a date for reporting or filtering directly inside the WHERE clause:
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PETRESCUE WHERE MONTH(RESCUE_DATE) = 5;
🔹 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗰 (𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗘_𝗔𝗗𝗗): Accurately shifts dates forward or backward by a set interval without worrying about 30-day vs. 31-day months:
  SELECT DATE_ADD(RESCUE_DATE, INTERVAL 3 DAY) FROM PETRESCUE;
🔹 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 (𝗖𝗨𝗥𝗥𝗘𝗡𝗧_𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗘): Uses the server's live system date to calculate exact elapsed time:
  SELECT (CURRENT_DATE - RESCUE_DATE) FROM PETRESCUE;

📂 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝗦𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆:

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟴 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 (𝗡𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀)

Try writing WHERE salary > AVG(salary) in SQL and the database immediately throws an "Invalid use of aggregate function" error. Try selecting EMP_ID, SALARY, AVG(SALARY) without grouping, and it fails again.

Today, I learned how wrapping a second SELECT statement inside parentheses—a Subquery—solves both blockers cleanly.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲: Computes the aggregate metric in an inner query first so the outer query can filter against it:
  SELECT EMP_ID, FIRST_NAME, SALARY FROM EMPLOYEES WHERE SALARY < (SELECT AVG(SALARY) FROM EMPLOYEES);
🔹 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧 𝗟𝗶𝘀𝘁: Compares individual row values side-by-side against the overall company average without collapsing rows:
  SELECT EMP_ID, SALARY, (SELECT AVG(SALARY) FROM EMPLOYEES) AS AVG_SALARY FROM EMPLOYEES;

🚀 𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟵 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆: 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀 (𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 & 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘀)

A single missing WHERE condition in a multi-table query can multiply 1,000 employees by 50 departments into 50,000 useless rows (a Cartesian Product).

In real databases, employee records and department details live in separate tables. Today, I practiced two ways to pull connected data across tables accurately.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀: Uses the output of a query on the DEPARTMENTS table as a filter inside the EMPLOYEES query:
  SELECT * FROM employees WHERE DEP_ID IN (SELECT DEP_ID_DEP FROM departments WHERE LOC_ID = 'L0002');
🔹 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘀: Lists multiple tables in FROM and links their matching Primary/Foreign Keys inside the WHERE clause to prevent a Cartesian Product:
  SELECT * FROM employees, departments WHERE employees.DEP_ID = departments.DEP_ID_DEP;
🔹 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗔𝗹𝗶𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: Gives tables short nicknames (like E and D) to keep multi-table queries clean and readable:
  SELECT E.EMP_ID, D.DEP_NAME FROM employees E, departments D WHERE E.DEP_ID = D.DEP_ID_DEP;

Writing standalone SQL queries is great for pulling data, but connecting SQL directly to Python inside a Jupyter Notebook lets you query, clean, and visualize data in one unified workflow.

Today, I mapped out the 4 standard API calls that happen behind the scenes every single time a Python script talks to a database.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:

🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟰-𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗗𝗕𝗠𝗦 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄:
  1. Connect: Authenticate and open a session with the DBMS.
  2. Build & Send: Pass the SQL query as a text string buffer via API.
  3. Check Status: Fetch the returned rows and handle any execution errors.
  4. Disconnect: Close the connection to free up database resources.

Before learning Python's DB-API, I wondered if switching from MySQL to PostgreSQL meant rewriting all my database code from scratch. Today, I learned how two core objects—Connections and Cursors—standardize database programming across Python.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:
🔹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗢𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 (𝗦𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿): Manages authentication and transactions using 4 key methods: .cursor(), .commit() to save changes, .rollback() to undo errors, and .close() to free memory.
🔹 𝗖𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗿 𝗢𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 (𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗲-𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗥𝗼𝘄𝘀): Executes SQL queries and scrolls through fetched results row-by-row. Multiple cursors on the same connection are not isolated—changes made by one are immediately visible to others.
🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟱-𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗗𝗕-𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻:

  cur = conn.cursor()
  cur.execute("SELECT * FROM employees;")
  rows = cur.fetchall()
  conn.close()

Numbers buried inside a raw CSV file rarely tell the full story. Today, I built an end-to-end Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) pipeline: loading a CSV into SQLite, querying it into Pandas, and spotting extreme outliers visually.

💡 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆:

  data = pd.read_csv('mcdonalds_menu.csv')
  conn = sqlite3.connect('mcdonalds.db')
  data.to_sql('mcdonalds_nutrition', conn)
  df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM mcdonalds_nutrition", conn)

🔹 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗻: Using swarmplot() for categorical distributions, jointplot() to check Protein vs. Fat correlation (r = 0.81), and boxplot() to highlight extreme sugar outliers.
